newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mideast peace worries dampen Cairo bourse - brokers.
newsitem.headline: Mideast peace worries dampen Cairo bourse - brokers.

text.p: Middle East peace worries sidelined some foreigners investing in the Cairo bourse, clearing the way for local investors who picked their way through cements and millers, brokers said on Wednesday.

Almost all the actively traded stocks ended lower but the Capital Market Authority (CMA) all-share index, supported by heavyweight stocks in the banking sector, inched up 2.19 points to 389.17 points.
Turnover was a low 49.91 million pounds ($14.70 million).

"Local funds are the ones with the buying power and they are buying large tranches, particularly in the cements. But the foreign investors are holding back because of the political situation," said Mohammad Abdallah of brokers Intercapital.
"No one is pulling out but no one new is coming in at this point because of the troubles in the peace process. The peace process was one of the points we used to attract foreigners," he added.
Egypt made peace with Israel in 1979 but brokers said foreign investors tend to regard the region as a whole and not as individual countries.
The Palestinian-Israeli peace process is currently deadlocked over a decision by the Jewish state to build a new settlement in the disputed Arab eastern quarter of Jerusalem.
Fertiliser firm Egyptian Financial and Industrial was the most actively traded firm, with shares worth 8.58 million pounds trading.
Brokers said the firm's forecast of good 1996/7 results and rumours that it would soon takeover a smaller competitor had spurred trading but shares ended 1.00 lower at 215.50 pounds.

Amriyah Cement was the busiest share in the active cement sector with 4.37 million pounds of turnover. It was closely followed by Helwan Portland Cement but Amriyah ended marginally higher at 88.5 while Helwan fell 0.5 to 79.5.
"The cements and the mills are the most liquid sectors and that is why they are active when the market is quiet," Abdallah said. "The cements are more stable so they see more trade."
Millers ended mixed with North Cairo Flour Mills leading the way in terms of volume. The share ended unchanged at 192 with 2.31 million shares changing hands.

Brokers said trading in Commercial International Bank (CIB) had propped up the CMA index against the losing shares. CIB gained 3.55 to 90 pounds on institutional buying which helped push the index higher as well.
The index for openly traded firms rose to 605.02 points from 598.17 points on Monday and the index for rarely traded "closed" firms rose to 268.37 points from 267.78.
Out of the 89 shares traded, 34 gained, 36 lost and 20 ended unchanged.
